detail:
How Much Does a 61-Year-Old Federal Retiree Need in the TSP to Collect $8,000 a Month With a Pension?
Joel South
Sun, November 15, 2026 at 9:32 AM EST 6 min read

Quick Read

A $70,000 pension leaves a $26,000 annual gap on an $8,000 monthly budget, requiring roughly $743,000 in the TSP at a 3.5% withdrawal rate.

Higher withdrawal rates shrink the needed balance to $433,000 at 6% or $260,000 at 10%, but they push money outside the TSP and erode principal.

Pension COLAs are missing until 62 and capped afterward, while taxes cut take-home pay, so a growing gap favors the lower withdrawal rate.

Many financial professionals are salespeople paid on what they push, not whether you end up wealthier. A fiduciary is the opposite. The SEC legally requires them to put your interests first. A 61-year-old federal retiree with a $70,000 annual pension already covers most of an $8,000 monthly budget. The Thrift Savings Plan only has to fill the rest, and that reduces the required balance a lot.

24/7 Wall St.

Annualized, $8,000 per month comes to $96,000 a year. That is above the $81,905 the average U.S. household spent in 2025. Take away the pension and the TSP has to produce $26,000 a year. Divide that gap by your withdrawal rate and you get the balance you need.

Three Withdrawal Rates, Three Very Different Balances
Conservative: 3.5% Requires About $743,000

$26,000 divided by 0.035 equals roughly $743,000. Inside the TSP, this usually means a stock-heavy mix of the C, S and I Funds, with the G Fund as ballast. The draw stays below what a diversified portfolio has typically earned over long stretches, so the principal can keep growing and the withdrawal can rise with it. Safe money pays well right now too: the 10-year Treasury yields 5%. This level needs the most capital and carries the least risk of running dry.

------

No sales call. Find out where you stand.

------

Moderate: 6% Requires About $433,000

$26,000 divided by 0.06 equals roughly $433,000. No TSP fund yields 6%, so getting there means selling shares or rolling part of the balance into an IRA that holds REITs, preferred shares, covered call funds or high-dividend equity funds. The tradeoff: income growth stalls, covered call strategies cap your upside and the payout falls behind inflation over a 30-year retirement.

Splitting $90,000 evenly across Amcor, UPS and Ford would generate about $5,000 a year in dividends, an average yield near 6%.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Three companies behind everyday packaging, parcel delivery, and pickup trucks all pay quarterly dividends. Had you put $30,000 into each of these three (a packaging maker, a parcel carrier, and an automaker), the $90,000 total would return about $5,067 a year in passive income.

RiverNorthPhotography / Getty Images

For retirees living off a portfolio, that cash shows up on a schedule, no matter what the market does. Here's what a $30,000 stake in each of these three high-yield names would return using each company's latest regular quarterly dividend, annualized at Nov. 13, 2026 prices, so they'll shift as prices and dividends change.

Ford Motor Turns Pickups Into a 5.03% Yield

Stock #3: Ford Motor (NYSE:F)

Yield (forward, regular dividend only): 5.03%

Shares for $30,000: 2,516.78

Annual Passive Income: ~$1,510

Ford makes gas and hybrid vehicles, sells work trucks and vans through Ford Pro, develops EVs in Model e, and loans to buyers through Ford Credit. The regular dividend has stayed at $0.15 every quarter in 2026, and the latest one is due Dec. 1. The larger payments in February 2024 ($0.33) and February 2025 ($0.30) aren't counted here.

The yield is high mostly because the stock trades at about 4 times free cash flow. In the third quarter, Ford returned $4.7 billion of adjusted free cash flow and ended the period with $25.3 billion in cash. It also reaffirmed full-year guidance of $6.0 billion to $7.0 billion. Uneven earnings remain the chief concern, as Ford posted a $1.327 billion second-quarter net loss after special charges, and management expects Model e to lose about $4 billion this year.

NEW YORK, November 13, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Citibank, N.A. is announcing the redemption, in whole, constituting $2,200,000,000 of its 4.876% Fixed Rate / Floating Rate Notes due 2027 (the "fixed rate / floating rate notes") (ISIN: US17325FBL13) and $800,000,000 of its Floating Rate Notes due 2027 (the "floating rate notes" and together with the fixed rate / floating rate notes, the "notes") (ISIN: US17325FBM95).

The redemption date for the notes is November 19, 2026 (the "redemption date"). The cash redemption price for the notes payable on the redemption date will equal par plus accrued and unpaid interest to, but excluding, the redemption date.

The redemptions announced today are consistent with Citibank's liability management strategy and reflect its ongoing efforts to enhance the efficiency of its funding and capital structure. Citibank will continue to consider opportunities to redeem or repurchase securities, based on several factors, including without limitation, the economic value, regulatory changes, potential impact on Citibank's net interest margin and borrowing costs, the overall remaining tenor of Citibank's debt portfolio, capital impact, as well as overall market conditions.

Beginning on the redemption date, interest will no longer accrue on the notes.

Citibank, N.A. is the paying agent for the notes.

Is Citi Wrong to Give Up on Roblox? It Trades at 4.9x Sales, Below Its 5-Year Average ©@Santri Bisa Desain from Bu Rezkia via Canva
Key Takeaways

Citi downgraded Roblox to Neutral from Buy and kept its $55 target. It pointed to fading interest in the hit game Steal an Egg and to the launch of Take-Two Interactive's Grand Theft Auto VI.

Roblox's own fourth-quarter guide doesn't count on recent hits repeating, and it builds in a modest hit from GTA VI.

Citi's target is 7% above the Nov. 12 close and 10% above the consensus, while the stock trades at 4.9x forward sales, below its 5-year average of 7.7x.

Neutral looks like the right rating, since analysts' 2027 loss estimate is still widening while Roblox spends more on AI and on marketing to adults.

Roblox (RBLX:NYSE) just lost one of its bulls. Citi analyst Jason Bazinet downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy on Nov. 13 and kept his $55 price target, 7% above the Nov. 12 close of $51.42. The stock is down 51% from a year earlier, but it's up 45% from its Aug. 12 closing low.

His case is about the next few months: Steal an Egg, this summer's viral hit, is fading, and Take-Two Interactive (TTWO:NASDAQ) launches Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov. 19.

A Summer Hit Is Cooling at Roblox

Steal an Egg didn't stop Roblox's daily users from falling 9% from a year earlier in the third quarter. Citi sees no new hit taking its place, and it expects GTA VI to pull attention and playtime away from Roblox. It thinks fourth-quarter bookings could land a bit below the middle of Roblox's guide for a 10% to 15% drop. Take-Two, for its part, expects net bookings of $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion in its fiscal year ending March 2027, with GTA VI in it.

Roblox Already Planned for Both

CFO Naveen Chopra said on the call that some recent strength came from "big hit games that have grown quickly on the platform" and Halloween updates, adding, "for guidance purposes, we don't assume that those things will necessarily repeat in the coming weeks." The same guide, which sent the stock down 18% on Oct. 30, does "build in a modest headwind from the release of GTA in the quarter." So the guide was already cautious on both worries.

Analysts have already done most of their cutting. The consensus target has fallen from $146 a year ago to $50, about where the stock trades.

Key Takeaways

A fund with $1.82 billion in US stocks filed its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 on Nov. 6, and its three biggest new or added positions were all financials: AIG, Carlyle and Citigroup.

AIG became the fund's largest US holding after a 50% addition, its Carlyle stake grew 34%, and Citigroup was a new position.

Wall Street's average targets sit 7% above today's price for AIG, 25% for Carlyle and 21% for Citigroup, but Carlyle's has been cut since February while Citigroup's has risen over the year.

Citigroup is the best of the three buys, with its returns climbing and even the lowest analyst target above today's price.

Algebris (UK)'s three biggest adds of the third quarter all came from one corner of the US market: financials. Its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 6, shows $1.82 billion of US stocks across 72 positions, and the top three new or added stakes were American International Group (AIG:NYSE), Carlyle (CG:NASDAQ) and Citigroup (C:NYSE).

AIG has already had its run

AIG was the fund's largest US holding on Sept. 30: 1.85 million shares worth $138 million, 7.6% of its 13F stocks, after a 50% addition in the quarter. The stock is up 11% since the quarter ended. In between, AIG reported third-quarter adjusted after-tax income of $2.06 a diluted share on Nov. 3, with net premiums written up 8% in constant dollars and a core operating return on equity of 11.1%.

Analysts see much less room from here. Their average target of $88.55, from 22 analysts, is 7% above today's price, and it has barely moved in a year:

American International Group (AIG): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

AIG trades at about 10x forward earnings. With the Street's average target stuck near $88 all year, a bigger gain from here needs AIG to grow faster than analysts already expect.

Carlyle comes with far more upside on paper. The fund added 34% to its stake, ending September with 2.57 million shares worth $102 million, 5.6% of its 13F stocks and its No. 2 holding.
